title: Write a cert-manager ClusterIssuer and Certificate
intro: identity-tutorial-009 debugged cert-manager objects that already existed. Now write the two a new service needs: an issuer that knows how to get certificates from Let's Encrypt, and a Certificate asking for one.

steps.prompt:
Write clusterissuer.yaml:
- apiVersion cert-manager.io/v1, kind ClusterIssuer, named letsencrypt-prod
- spec.acme.server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
- spec.acme.email: platform@example.com
- spec.acme.privateKeySecretRef.name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
- spec.acme.solvers: one entry, an http01 solver whose ingress has ingressClassName: nginx
steps.hint:
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx
A ClusterIssuer has no namespace.
steps.solution:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx
steps.explanation: An issuer any namespace can use, which proves domain ownership over HTTP through the nginx ingress controller.
steps.why: The email receives expiry warnings, which is your last line of defence if renewal breaks. privateKeySecretRef is where cert-manager stores its ACME account key; it creates that Secret itself. The solver's ingress class must be the controller that really receives traffic for your hostnames, or challenges return 404 (the tutorial's failure). Write a second issuer pointing at the staging server (acme-staging-v02) and use it for anything that requests certificates repeatedly, so a loop can't use up production's rate limit (identity-incident-005). For wildcard certificates, or services not reachable from the internet, use a dns01 solver instead.

steps.prompt:
Write certificate.yaml:
- apiVersion cert-manager.io/v1, kind Certificate, named shop-tls, in namespace shop
- spec.secretName: shop-tls
- spec.dnsNames: shop.example.com and www.shop.example.com
- spec.issuerRef: name letsencrypt-prod, kind ClusterIssuer
- spec.privateKey.rotationPolicy: Always
steps.hint:
spec:
  secretName: shop-tls
  dnsNames:
    - shop.example.com
    - www.shop.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  privateKey:
    rotationPolicy: Always
steps.solution:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: shop-tls
  namespace: shop
spec:
  secretName: shop-tls
  dnsNames:
    - shop.example.com
    - www.shop.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  privateKey:
    rotationPolicy: Always
steps.explanation: A request for one certificate covering both names, stored in the Secret shop-tls and renewed automatically.
steps.why: issuerRef.kind matters: it defaults to Issuer (namespaced), so leaving it out makes cert-manager look for an Issuer called letsencrypt-prod in namespace shop, find nothing, and wait for ever. Every name clients use must be in dnsNames, because that list becomes the certificate's SAN (identity-tutorial-008). rotationPolicy Always generates a new private key at each renewal, so a key that leaked stops being useful. The Ingress then refers to the Secret in its tls section. An annotation on the Ingress (cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer) can create this Certificate for you; writing it explicitly keeps it visible in Git and independent of the Ingress.
